nameStory: This tiny spider doesn't have a widely recognized common name, so it's known by its scientific name Disembolus corneliae. The genus name 'Disembolus' comes from Greek words meaning 'twice thrown' or 'double cast,' likely referring to some aspect of the male spider's mating structures. The species was named 'corneliae' to honor someone named Cornelia, though the exact story behind this dedication has been lost to scientific history.
description: Disembolus corneliae is a minuscule dwarf spider that belongs to the sheet web weaver family. Like other dwarf spiders, it's incredibly small - typically measuring less than 2-3 millimeters in body length, about the size of a pinhead. These spiders are so tiny that you'd need a magnifying glass to see their details clearly. They're part of one of the largest spider families and are master architects of delicate sheet webs.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small spider, usually under 3mm in body length - about the size of a small ant or pinhead, requiring magnification to see details clearly

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates tiny, flat sheet webs that feel delicate and papery when accidentally brushed, often with sticky trap lines above the sheet surface

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with relatively long, thin legs that appear almost thread-like when viewed through a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Runs upside-down beneath its sheet web when disturbed, moving with quick, jerky motions that can make it hard to follow with the naked eye

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Builds webs close to the ground in protected microhabitats like leaf litter edges or among low vegetation where humidity stays consistent

habitat: This rare dwarf spider is found in sheltered ground-level habitats throughout New England, though it's been documented very infrequently. Look for their tiny sheet webs among leaf litter, low-growing vegetation, or in the protected spaces near fallen logs where moisture levels remain stable. They prefer areas with some canopy cover that provide protection from direct sunlight and drying winds.

seasonality.spring: Adults may become active as temperatures warm, building new sheet webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation. Look for tiny webs close to the ground level.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found. Their small sheet webs may be more noticeable when decorated with morning dew.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs, and egg sacs may be present in or near the web structures. Adults may still be active during warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as eggs or juveniles in protected microhabitats. Adult activity ceases during cold periods, making winter observations extremely unlikely.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it's only been officially documented once in the entire region! You'd have a better chance of finding a four-leaf clover than spotting one of these tiny web builders, making any sighting a genuine scientific treasure.
confusionNotes: Due to its extremely small size and rarity, this spider is most likely to be confused with other tiny dwarf spiders in the same family. The key difference is that you'll need expert-level magnification and specialized knowledge to distinguish between different Linyphiidae species - most are simply too small for reliable field identification by general observers.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific community still has much to learn about this species' ecology and distribution in New England. Its extreme rarity in collections might reflect either genuine scarcity or the difficulty of finding and identifying such tiny spiders. Citizen scientists should photograph any extremely small spiders they find, as every observation could contribute valuable data.
compareHints: Since this is the only Disembolus species documented in New England, compare it with other dwarf spiders in the Linyphiidae family. Most can only be reliably distinguished by examining male reproductive structures under high magnification. In the field, focus on web structure and microhabitat preferences rather than trying to identify the spider itself to species level.
